lead: A bevel gear pair joins shafts whose axes meet, usually at 90°. The teeth are cut on cones, so a tooth is large at the outer end and shrinks towards the cone apex. Design treats each bevel gear as an equivalent spur gear drawn on its back cone, applies the Lewis and Buckingham checks with a correction for the taper, and takes the tooth load at the middle of the face. Straight bevel gears drive hand drills, differentials and right-angle drives.
prereq: You need: the Lewis and Buckingham checks of spur gear design.

blocks.text: The two pitch cones roll on each other without slip and share one apex. The pitch angle γ is the half-angle of a pitch cone, measured from the gear's own axis; γ1 for the pinion, γ2 for the gear. The shaft angle Σ = γ1 + γ2. For Σ = 90°, tan γ1 = z1/z2 and γ2 = 90° − γ1. Some syllabi write δ for the pitch angle.

Sizes are given at the large end. The module m, the pitch diameters d = mz, the addendum and the dedendum are all measured there. The cone distance R (some books write A0) is the slant length from the apex to the large end of the pitch cone: R = d1/(2 sin γ1), which for 90° shafts is √((d1/2)² + (d2/2)²). The face width b is measured along the cone; keep b ≤ R/3 (or about 10m, whichever is smaller), because the tooth tapers to nothing at the apex and a wide face only adds weak, small-end tooth.

The back cone is the cone at the large end whose surface is at right angles to the pitch cone. Unrolled flat, it shows the teeth as spur teeth on a circle of radius r/cos γ. That equivalent spur gear has the virtual (formative) number of teeth zv = z/cos γ. This is the Tredgold approximation; Y is read for zv.

The tooth force acts near the middle of the face. The mean radius of the pinion is r<sub>m1</sub> = d<sub>1</sub>/2 − (b sin γ<sub>1</sub>)/2, and the tangential force is F<sub>t</sub> = T/r<sub>m1</sub> with T in N·mm. Because the tooth shrinks towards the apex, the beam strength of the large-end tooth is reduced by the factor (1 − b/R):
S<sub>b</sub> = σ<sub>b</sub> b m Y (1 − b/R)
blocks.where: S<sub>b</sub> is in N; σ<sub>b</sub> in N/mm²; b, m and R in mm; Y for z<sub>v</sub>. The first sizing uses C<sub>v</sub> = 3/(3 + v) and F<sub>eff</sub> = C<sub>s</sub> F<sub>t</sub>/C<sub>v</sub>, with v the pitch line velocity at the large end.

blocks.text: Buckingham's dynamic load is the spur gear formula, F<sub>d</sub> = 21v(Ceb + F<sub>t</sub>)/(21v + √(Ceb + F<sub>t</sub>)), and F<sub>eff</sub> = C<sub>s</sub> F<sub>t</sub> + F<sub>d</sub>. The wear strength uses the virtual gears and a factor 0.75 for the shorter, tapering contact:
Sw = 0.75 b Q′ d1 K / cos γ1 with Q′ = 2zv2/(zv1 + zv2), d1 the large-end pinion diameter in mm and K = 0.16(BHN/100)² for steel. Both checks need S ≥ fs Feff.

Straight bevel teeth also push the shafts apart and along their axes. For pressure angle φ, the pinion carries an axial thrust F<sub>a1</sub> = F<sub>t</sub> tan φ sin γ<sub>1</sub> and a radial force F<sub>r1</sub> = F<sub>t</sub> tan φ cos γ<sub>1</sub>. For a 90° pair the pinion's axial force is the gear's radial force and the other way round. The pinion's thrust always points away from the cone apex, towards its large end.

items: Fix the ratio and choose z<sub>1</sub> so that z<sub>v1</sub> is above the undercut limit; find γ<sub>1</sub>, γ<sub>2</sub> and z<sub>v1</sub>, z<sub>v2</sub>.
Choose the weaker member from σ<sub>b</sub> Y; size the module with S<sub>b</sub> = f<sub>s</sub> C<sub>s</sub> F<sub>t</sub>/C<sub>v</sub>, using b = R/3 or 10m, and round up to a standard module.
With the module fixed, find d<sub>1</sub>, d<sub>2</sub>, R, b ≤ R/3, r<sub>m1</sub> and F<sub>t</sub>.
Find F<sub>d</sub> and F<sub>eff</sub> = C<sub>s</sub> F<sub>t</sub> + F<sub>d</sub>; check S<sub>b</sub> and S<sub>w</sub> against f<sub>s</sub> F<sub>eff</sub>.
Find F<sub>a</sub> and F<sub>r</sub> on each shaft and pass them to the bearing selection.

blocks.text: Spiral bevel and hypoid gears (curved teeth, offset axes) follow their own standards.

spec.aria: Pinion and gear pitch cones from a common apex with pitch angles 26.57 and 63.43 degrees, cone distance 89.44 millimetres, face width 25 millimetres and mean radius 34.41 millimetres.

examples.question: A 90° straight bevel pair has z<sub>1</sub> = 20, z<sub>2</sub> = 40, module 4 mm at the large end and face width 25 mm. Find d<sub>1</sub>, d<sub>2</sub>, γ<sub>1</sub>, γ<sub>2</sub>, R, the mean pinion radius, the mean module and both virtual tooth numbers.
steps: Pitch diameters: d<sub>1</sub> = 4 × 20 = 80 mm, d<sub>2</sub> = 4 × 40 = 160 mm.
Pitch angles: tan γ<sub>1</sub> = 20/40 = 0.5, so γ<sub>1</sub> = 26.565°, γ<sub>2</sub> = 63.435°.
Cone distance: R = √(40² + 80²) = √8000 = 89.44 mm. R/3 = 29.81 mm, so b = 25 mm is allowed.
Mean module: m<sub>m</sub> = m(R − b/2)/R = 4 × 76.94/89.44 = 3.441 mm (check: 2r<sub>m1</sub>/z<sub>1</sub> = 68.82/20 = 3.441 mm).

examples.question: The pair of the first example transmits 3 kW at 1000 rpm of the pinion. Both gears are steel, σ<sub>b</sub> = 200 N/mm², 350 BHN; C<sub>s</sub> = 1.25, e = 0.010 mm, C = 11 400 N/mm², φ = 20°. Find the factors of safety in bending and wear, and the pinion's axial and radial forces.
examples.answer: Factor of safety 1.59 in bending and 1.63 in wear, both above 1.5; pinion thrust 135.5 N and radial force 271.0 N.

traps: Using z instead of z<sub>v</sub> = z/cos γ for the form factor and for Q′.
Taking the torque at the large-end radius. The load acts near the mean radius, which is smaller, so the true F<sub>t</sub> is larger; the large-end radius makes the design unsafe.
Leaving out (1 − b/R) in the beam strength, or making b larger than R/3: the extra face is small, weak tooth near the apex.
Adding the pitch angles to 180°. They add to the shaft angle, 90° for a right-angle pair.
Swapping the force components: for the pinion the axial force has sin γ<sub>1</sub> and the radial force cos γ<sub>1</sub>.

quiz.q: For a 90° pair, relate the pinion pitch angle to the tooth numbers.
quiz.a: tan γ<sub>1</sub> = z<sub>1</sub>/z<sub>2</sub> and γ<sub>2</sub> = 90° − γ<sub>1</sub>.

quiz.q: Define cone distance and back cone.
quiz.a: The cone distance R is the slant length of the pitch cone from the apex to the large end. The back cone is the cone at the large end whose elements are perpendicular to the pitch cone.

quiz.q: Why is the form factor read for z/cos γ?
quiz.a: Unrolled, the back cone shows the teeth as spur teeth on a circle of radius r/cos γ, so the tooth shape is that of a spur gear with z/cos γ teeth (Tredgold's approximation).

quiz.q: What does the factor (1 − b/R) in the beam strength allow for?
quiz.a: The tooth shrinks towards the apex, so its strength falls along the face. The factor reduces the strength of the large-end tooth to that of the whole tapering tooth.

quiz.q: A 90° pair has z<sub>1</sub> = 18, z<sub>2</sub> = 36 and m = 5 mm. Find γ<sub>1</sub>, R and the largest face width.
quiz.a: d<sub>1</sub> = 90 mm, d<sub>2</sub> = 180 mm. γ<sub>1</sub> = tan⁻¹0.5 = 26.57°. R = √(45² + 90²) = 100.62 mm. b ≤ R/3 = 33.5 mm (and 10m = 50 mm), so b = 33 mm at most.

quiz.q: F<sub>t</sub> = 2000 N, φ = 20°, γ<sub>1</sub> = 26.57°. Find the pinion's axial thrust.
A student computes F<sub>t</sub> from the torque at the large-end radius. Is the design safe? Explain.
quiz.a: Unsafe. For the same torque a larger radius gives a smaller force. The real load acts near the mean radius, so the true F<sub>t</sub> is larger and the stresses are underestimated.

beyond: Not for the exam. Most vehicle axles use spiral bevel or hypoid sets, which run quieter and allow an offset pinion. They are cut on specialist generators and checked by the contact pattern seen under light load. Search for spiral bevel contact pattern, hypoid offset and ISO 10300.
